evidence_set: Post-marketing surveillance by an independent steering committee that the drug's sponsor, Ortho-McNeil Pharmaceuticals, set up on the recommendation of the FDA's Drug Abuse Advisory Committee when tramadol (Ultram) was marketed in the USA without scheduling. Reports came from spontaneous adverse-event reports to the company and the FDA (MedWatch: patients, pharmacists, physicians) and from a network of 110 NIDA-funded researchers and 145 other experts on drug use with access to about 250,000 people at risk for drug misuse, offered $75 for each completed questionnaire (average response 48.7% over 20 quarters); a subcommittee classified every report with DSM-IV-based ratings. No group of people who stopped tramadol without withdrawal, or who stopped another opioid, was studied (editors' reading of the design).

Withdrawal ratings (21 typical, 22 atypical) were used only when there was no drug-seeking or other evidence of 'abuse'; reports with withdrawal and drug-seeking were rated as 'abuse'. Because unusual symptoms appeared as the study progressed, all withdrawal cases of 1995–2000 were rescored as typical or atypical. Typical withdrawal needed at least three DSM-IV opioid withdrawal symptoms; atypical withdrawal also had a strong component of other CNS disturbances, and is described as always accompanied by typical symptoms (3.1), as often combined with them (Table 2, footnote b) and, in the Discussion (p. 238), as occurring in addition to or in place of them. The authors say 'atypical' is a descriptor, not a claim that there are two syndromes. No check of agreement between raters is reported.
2.2 Detailed methods, 4th and 5th paragraphs (p. 235, the 5th continuing p. 236); Table 1 (p. 235); Table 2, footnotes a and b, and 3.1, 1st paragraph (p. 236); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 238)

The abstract says withdrawal of either type made up nearly 40% of all adverse events reported, and the Discussion calls it the most prevalent adverse event (nearly 40% of total cases); Table 3 gives 33%, and 644 of the same 1,248 reports were rated as 'abuse' (3.2, p. 237).
Abstract (p. 233); Table 3 and 3.2, 1st paragraph (p. 237); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (p. 238)

Typical withdrawal symptoms listed: abdominal cramps, anxiety, bone pain, depression, diarrhoea, goose flesh, insomnia, tearing, nausea, restlessness, runny nose and sweating (no frequencies). Among the 55 atypical cases: severe anxiety and panic attacks 32.8%; unusual CNS symptoms (confusion, delusions, depersonalization, derealization, paranoia) 27.2%; unusual sensory phenomena (numbness, tingling, paresthesia, tinnitus) 25.4%; hallucinations (tactile, visual, auditory) 20.0%; the total exceeds 100% because several were reported together. Editors' calculation: the nearest counts of 55 (18, 15, 14 and 11) give 32.7%, 27.3%, 25.5% and 20.0% when rounded, or 32.7%, 27.2%, 25.4% and 20.0% when cut off; no single rule gives all four printed percentages, so they cannot all come from 55.

Age was known for only 139 of 455 withdrawal cases (a total that matches neither 422 nor 546), with no figures given; sex was known in 82% of typical and 87% of atypical cases, of whom about 56% were women (55.8% and 56.3%); the authors say this suggests both types may be more common in women, but that the data do not appear to establish any relation between sex and withdrawal.

Length of exposure was known in about 50% of withdrawal cases: many followed brief exposures of 3–4 days, with no clustering after long exposure (no counts). Maintenance dose was known in 63% of typical cases (50–2,000 mg a day; 92% at or below the maximum recommended level of 400 mg a day) and 78% of atypical cases (50–1,300 mg a day); the paper gives 25% of all atypical cases as above 400 mg, three times the 8% of typical cases, without saying whether the base is all atypical cases or those with a known dose (no counts or test). Atypical cases tended to last longer and to be harder to manage.

Withdrawal followed abrupt discontinuation, which the authors say many physicians did despite the label's warning, and in some instances dose reductions or a tapered stop. Most physicians described relatively mild cases that they monitored without treatment and that usually resolved in 2 or 3 days; as severity increased, treatment was often necessary. The committee's clinicians drew on about 75 consultations; no counts are given, and outcomes only in general terms.

The authors say the atypical symptoms were more like those reported on stopping SSRI antidepressants than on stopping opioids, may relate to tramadol's reported noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake inhibition, which remains to be determined, and could be misdiagnosed as psychosis or delirium. They report no difference between typical and atypical cases in age, sex, length of exposure or history of drug misuse (figures shown only for sex), so they could define no feature that would indicate who may be at risk of atypical symptoms, with one possible exception: more atypical cases had been at doses above 400 mg a day (25% against 8%).

evidence_set: 1006 Finnish autopsy cases toxicologically investigated at the Department of Forensic Medicine, University of Helsinki, in 1995–2000, whose cause of death a forensic pathologist had established as poisoning by alcohol, a single drug or both (where both, the more important cause cited first on the death certificate). Femoral blood taken at autopsy into 1% sodium fluoride and kept at 4 °C; alcohol measured in every sample and a broad drug screen in about 83% of cases, at the pathologist's request; blood alcohol given in parts per thousand, mass per mass. The nine drugs were those present in at least 20 fatal poisonings of each type; limit of quantitation 0.02 mg/L for temazepam. Each drug's lowest included concentration was the bottom of its therapeutic range, except temazepam, counted from 0.1 mg/L because effects can occur below the therapeutic level; mixed poisonings needed blood alcohol of at least 0.50. Caffeine, nicotine and small amounts of 2-propanol and acetone were allowed in the cases; the 615 deaths from alcohol alone were free of other analytes in the screens; low concentrations (under 1 mg/L) of diazepam, chlordiazepoxide, nordazepam or demoxepam were allowed in the mixed groups.

Temazepam group split at 0.7 mg/L (the divide counted in the low half): 28 deaths at or below, median blood alcohol 2.9; 29 above, median 2.1; printed point estimate of the difference 0.9 (the printed medians differ by 0.8), P < 0.001. With the 18 deaths in which temazepam was only below its therapeutic range (under 0.4 mg/L) set aside, the median blood alcohol in the remaining 39 was 2.2 (95% CI 2.1–2.5). The authors read the higher-concentration halves' lower medians as suggesting a positive concentration–effect relationship.

Temazepam is the only benzodiazepine among the nine drugs studied, which were those present in at least 20 fatal poisonings of each type. The authors cite their own earlier paper (reference 20: Alcohol Clin Exp Res 2002;26:956–959; not read here) as finding that temazepam lowered the blood alcohol at which a given share of alcohol poisonings occurs, while with diazepam, chlordiazepoxide or desmethyldiazepam at concentrations up to 1 mg/L the blood alcohol did not differ from pure alcohol poisonings, and say that in that study diazepam and chlordiazepoxide appeared significantly safer than temazepam with alcohol.

Printed differences in median blood alcohol from the alcohol-only deaths: citalopram 0.3 (P > 0.05), diltiazem 0.6 (P = 0.006), zopiclone 0.6, temazepam 0.8, levomepromazine 0.9, amitriptyline 1.5, propoxyphene 1.6, doxepin 1.6, promazine 1.9 (each P < 0.001). Fatal toxicity index (annual deaths divided by annual sales in defined daily doses per 1000 inhabitants per day): temazepam 0.9 (95% CI 0.7–1.1; 14.33 deaths and 15.95 sold a year) and zopiclone 0.9 (0.7–1.2), the lowest of the nine; promazine 120.8 (97.7–143.9), the highest. Temazepam's 14.33 deaths a year come to about 86 over the six years (editors' calculation), more than the 57 deaths with alcohol, so the index is not limited to deaths with alcohol. The authors say this division reflects not only acute toxicity but also how the drugs are used, some taken deliberately in overdose for intoxication or with suicidal intent, and that more information is needed to separate behaviour from the drugs' own toxicity.

evidence_set: Table 2: 13 studies in people with 'histories of drug abuse', 2 to 16 people each, men in all but one (Healey and Pickens 1983: men and women, n = 10); drug given orally and double-blind except two early studies; 11 of the 13 have the review's first author as co-author (editors' count from the reference list); four (Griffiths et al. 1976, Bigelow et al. 1976, Healey and Pickens 1983, Troisi et al. 1993) had no placebo comparison (editors' count). The text says comparisons within and across the studies suggest that the person's history is the most important single determinant, and that these studies almost invariably showed reinforcement: diazepam chosen over placebo on every occasion and oxazepam on 79% by 16 men; triazolam a reinforcer in 4 of 6 men and, in another study of 8 men, only before a relaxation task; lorazepam was chosen over buspirone by 7 of 8, but with no placebo the table calls it unclear whether lorazepam was a reinforcer. Doses (study conditions) were mostly far above those in Table 3 (editors' comparison), for example diazepam 50–400 mg, 40–160 mg and 40 or 80 mg in three studies; the text says higher doses were usually associated with greater reinforcing effects than lower doses.

Moderate social drinkers chose diazepam over placebo in three studies: 100% of choices (12 people), 73% (14) and 64% (30; buspirone 27% in 25 others); light drinkers tested in two of them (means of 12 and 4 drinks a week for the moderate and light drinkers of those two studies) chose it on 66% (a non-significant tendency, 18 people) and 40% (13), the light–moderate difference significant in the second. In both studies with light drinkers the moderate drinkers had significantly more weekly marijuana use (26% on average across the three studies), and a pooled analysis found that people who chose diazepam reported more current marijuana and lifetime stimulant use; the review says this was not investigated prospectively. Elsewhere it says that people with histories of moderate drinking and men with alcoholism showed increased sensitivity to the reinforcing and positive mood effects of benzodiazepines (no figures), and it calls the implications of moderate drinkers' preference for later risk unclear.

Anxious people, five double-blind studies, mixed: in the two with a single morning dose and a return to daily activities diazepam was not a reinforcer and placebo was preferred (Table 3 marks diazepam as a punisher in both; de Wit et al. 1986; McCracken et al. 1990, 14 people seeking treatment, 10 mg diazepam on 37% of sessions); the three giving control over time and total amount found preference: 65% of evening choice sessions in 22 anxious people against 45% in 23 controls (marginal, P = 0.06), with more capsules taken; 3 of 4 women with generalized anxiety disorder chose diazepam exclusively, and 11 of 14 people with generalized anxiety or panic disorder showed clear alprazolam preference, taking capsules 'as needed' for 4 weeks, most at low, stable rates. Insomnia: triazolam chosen on 86% of nights under a forced choice with placebo (three groups of 8, one per condition), but capsules taken on 77% and 80% of nights when only triazolam or only placebo was on offer, and in other studies placebo taken on more than 60% of nights, not different from triazolam. The review says a comparison of Table 3 studies, not investigated prospectively, suggests that benzodiazepines are more likely to function as reinforcers, or less likely as punishers, when people control the time and total amount.

evidence_set: The author states that most people, 70% to 90%, who use even the most stigmatized drugs, such as heroin and methamphetamine, do not meet criteria for a substance use disorder (DSM-5), which he describes as drug use causing significant distress and problems that impair functioning and says some people do experience; he cites only his own 2013 book and gives no survey, population, year, time frame or definition of who counts as using. He draws from it that addiction is a minority of drug effects that receives almost all the attention, and that if most people who use a drug do not become addicted, the drug cannot be blamed for causing addiction.

evidence_set: Number of the 24 reporting each complaint (placebo, MDMA, LSD, LSD + MDMA), 0–12 h: nausea 4, 14, 7, 11 (12–24 h: 1, 2, 2, 3; none before the dose); headache 11, 16, 17, 16; lack of energy 3, 12, 12, 15; loss of appetite 1, 13, 12, 16 (12–24 h: 0, 3, 4, 12); dry mouth 3, 12, 17, 17; teeth grinding or jaw rigidity 1, 9, 11, 14; trembling 1, 15, 5, 14; restlessness in legs 2, 9, 6, 12; heart palpitations 2, 9, 9, 10. No tests of these counts. The counts fit the results text (acute nausea more frequent with MDMA than LSD, p. 1842), not the discussion's statement that nausea was about as frequent with the combination as with either drug alone (p. 1845). Peak nausea ratings on the visual analogue scale ran the other way (article Table 1, p. 1843: placebo 1.0, MDMA 7.9, LSD 25 and LSD + MDMA 21% of the scale maximum; LSD and the combination higher than MDMA, p < 0.001 and p < 0.05, and not different from each other).
